title: Into thy hands (Psalm 30 [31])
hook: the line Jesus prayed as he died, prayed each night at Compline
tomorrow: Blessed are they whose sins are covered (Psalm 31 [32])

segments.voice: Yesterday, ori, my light, a psalm that turns on the lamp in a dark room. Your line was whom shall I fear. Today, a line for letting go.

A child at bedtime, in a house where someone prays, says a small memorized line, half asleep. A dying man in a hospital bed says a few last words. Sometimes they're the same kind of line. One sentence in scripture has been said at both moments, by children in bunk beds and monks in choir, by martyrs and, Luke's Gospel says, by Jesus himself. It's only a few words long, and it comes from Psalm 30 in the Douay, 31 in most Bibles.
screen: `THE LAST WORDS AT BEDTIME.` → `THE LAST WORDS AT DEATH.` → `THE SAME LINE.`

segments.voice: In the Douay-Rheims: "Into thy hands I commend my spirit: thou hast redeemed me, O Lord, the God of truth." Commend means to hand over, to entrust, the way you'd hand someone your child or your keys. The rest of the psalm is someone in real trouble: a net laid for their feet, friends who've turned away, a body worn out with grief. In the middle of it, this one line of handing over. Luke's Gospel says that as Jesus died, he cried out with a loud voice: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." He took the psalm's line and added one word at the front: Father. In Luke, those are his last words. Not a scream, a handing over. Then the line kept going. In the Acts of the Apostles, as Stephen, whom tradition calls the first martyr, is being stoned, he prays: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." The same handing over, now addressed to Jesus. Then the Church made it a nightly habit. For centuries at Compline, the prayer before sleep, monks and nuns have sung a short response built on this verse, In manus tuas, Domine: into your hands, Lord. Sleep, in the old way of thinking, is a small rehearsal for death: you close your eyes and hand yourself over, not knowing for certain you'll wake. So every night becomes practice for letting go. Jews have a neighboring line: the hymn Adon Olam, sung at bedtime and in the synagogue, ends by entrusting the spirit into God's hand.
screen: `COMMEND: TO HAND OVER.` · `FATHER, INTO THY HANDS.` · `STEPHEN: RECEIVE MY SPIRIT.` · `EVERY NIGHT AT COMPLINE.`

segments.voice: Let your hands rest open on your knees, palms up, and think of what you're carrying from today: the undone task, the worry, the person you're anxious about. One by one, picture setting each of them in open hands that aren't yours. If you pray, say the line, into thy hands I commend my spirit; if you don't, simply open your hands and let the day go.
Commend. To hand over, to entrust, the word at the heart of the psalm's line of handing over, prayed by Jesus as he died and by the Church every night. Today's word.
Your line: a small rehearsal for death. Said softly, it's a bedtime prayer. Rest easy.

howItsDone: Catholics who pray Night Prayer (Compline) say the short responsory 'Into your hands, Lord, I commend my spirit' every night; many also pray the line at a deathbed and teach it to children at bedtime.

notes: Douay Psalm 30:6 and Acts 7:58 wording: confirm against a Challoner edition (Acts 7:58 in the Douay numbering corresponds to 7:59 elsewhere).
Compline short responsory 'In manus tuas, Domine, commendo spiritum meum': in the Roman Breviary and in the current Liturgy of the Hours. Confirm.
Adon Olam ends with the line entrusting the spirit into God's hand, and is sung at bedtime and in services. Mentioned briefly as a neighbor. Confirm.
Sleep as a rehearsal for death: a common theme in Christian night prayer; hedged 'in the old way of thinking'.
Stephen also prays 'Lord, lay not this sin to their charge' (Acts 7:59 DR); paraphrased in the fork reveal.
